value.overview: The Ashy-throated Chlorospingus (Chlorospingus canigularis) is a small, active songbird of cool montane forests. It is olive-green above, with a distinctly gray or ashy throat and chest, contrasting facial markings, and yellowish to olive underparts. Often encountered in pairs or small mixed-species flocks, it searches foliage for insects and small fruits. Despite its former common name, it is classified with the New World sparrows in some modern taxonomies and with tanagers in others.
value.classification: The species belongs to the genus Chlorospingus. It is placed in the family Passerellidae by several modern taxonomies, although Chlorospingus species were historically treated as bush-tanagers in the family Thraupidae.
value.identification: This chlorospingus is a compact, short-tailed forest bird with mainly olive-green upperparts and a noticeable ash-gray throat. The head typically shows a darker crown and contrasting pale markings around the eye and cheek, while the lower breast and belly are more yellowish or olive. Its subdued colors help separate it from brighter montane tanagers. It is usually detected by its active movements through dense foliage and its sharp, high-pitched calls rather than by prolonged views.
value.rangeHabitat: The Ashy-throated Chlorospingus occurs in the mountains of Costa Rica and Panama and continues south through the northern Andes into South America. In Costa Rica it is a resident of highland and montane forest, especially humid evergreen forest, forest edges, second growth, and wooded clearings at middle to high elevations. It is regularly associated with the Cordilleras and other upland areas, including sites in the central highlands. It may also use shade-grown habitats and well-vegetated edges near intact forest.
value.migrationStatus: It is considered resident rather than migratory. In Costa Rica, birds are present year-round in suitable montane habitats, although local movements may occur with elevation, weather, food availability, or seasonal breeding conditions.
value.breeding: Reliable detailed information on its breeding biology is limited. Like related chlorospinguses, it is believed to nest in dense vegetation in montane forest, with the nest placed above the ground and the young fed by both adults. Breeding activity in Costa Rica is expected to be linked to the local rainy season, when insects and other food are abundant, but the precise nesting period and nest characteristics may vary among populations and are not sufficiently documented for a detailed account.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet consists mainly of insects and other small invertebrates, supplemented by small fruits and possibly seeds. It forages actively among leaves, twigs, vines, and shrubs, often joining mixed-species feeding flocks with other highland birds. The species usually picks prey from vegetation but may also make short movements to capture insects or reach fruiting plants.
value.behavior: The Ashy-throated Chlorospingus is energetic and social. It commonly travels in pairs, family groups, or mixed-species flocks, moving quickly through the middle and upper levels of forest vegetation. Its calls help maintain contact while the flock moves. It is generally more easily heard than seen because it remains within dense foliage, but its repeated movements and gray throat can make identification possible during close encounters.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not precisely quantified, and a detailed population trend is not well documented. The species is not currently considered globally threatened.
